title: Incident: Slack outage, January 2021
objective: Follow Slack's write-up of 4 January 2021: how a network problem, cold caches and autoscaling fed each other, and why the tools for fixing it were hit too.

sources.title: Slack Engineering: Slack's Outage on January 4th 2021 (Laura Nolan, 1 Feb 2021)

simplifies: Simplified to its key moments from Slack's own write-up (times PST). Some times are approximate in the write-up itself ("around 8:15am PST", "by around 9:15am PST"). AWS's Transit Gateways, the network links between Slack's networks, are shown as one box.

steps.caption: 4 January 2021 was the first working day after the holidays. Clients' caches had gone cold, so each client downloaded more data than usual when it first connected.
Error rates rose: only 99% of messages were being sent successfully, when the rate is usually over 99.999%. The network between Slack's systems was dropping packets.
A regular morning traffic peak met the packet loss. The web tier saturated and Slack became unavailable.

Autoscaling downscaled the web tier, and instances that couldn't reach their backends were marked unhealthy and replaced. Engineers turned downscaling off. Then saturated worker threads triggered a huge upscale: between 7:01 and 7:15, Slack tried to add 1,200 servers.

predict.prompt: Web servers are stuck waiting on a slow network, so their CPU use is low. Autoscaling uses CPU. What does it do?

options.text: Removes servers, because low CPU looks like too much capacity
options.explanation: Right. Slack's write-up says autoscaling downscaled the web tier while it was struggling.
Low CPU doesn't look like overload to a CPU-based rule.
Autoscaling reacts to what it measures, and it measured low CPU.

steps.caption: Provision-service hit two limits: the Linux open-files limit (the most significant) and an AWS quota. The dashboards were down too, because they reached their databases over the same network links, so engineers fell back to command-line tools and logs.

predict.prompt: 1,200 new servers all need setting up at once, over the same struggling network. What happens to the service that sets them up?

options.text: It sets them all up in seconds
options.explanation: It ran over the same degraded network and was never built for this spike.

options.text: It isn't needed: servers set themselves up
options.explanation: Each new instance is configured and tested by provision-service.

options.text: It's overloaded and hits limits, so many new servers come up broken
options.explanation: Right. Provision-service hit the Linux open-files limit and an AWS quota.

steps.caption: Provision-service recovered around 8:15, and by about 9:15 enough servers were working that Slack was degraded rather than down.
AWS had manually increased the network links' capacity; "by 10:40am PST" the change was rolled out everywhere, and errors and latency returned to normal.

Changes Slack listed: ask for the links to be scaled up before future holidays, move the dashboards next to their databases, load-test provision-service regularly, and review health checks and autoscaling.

quiz.prompt: Why did autoscaling make things worse at first?

options.explanation: It was on, and it acted on misleading signals.

options.text: It scaled on CPU, and servers waiting on a slow network use little CPU, so it removed servers when they were most needed
options.explanation: Right. A metric that's fine normally can point the wrong way in a strange failure.
Its first move was to remove them.

quiz.prompt: Why were Slack's dashboards unavailable during the outage?

options.explanation: They existed; they were in a different network from their databases.

options.text: Too many people were looking at them
options.explanation: The cause was the network path, not viewers.

options.text: They depended on the same network links that were failing
options.explanation: Right. Tools for fixing an outage shouldn't depend on the thing that's broken.
